title: Cold-start protocol for large sharded models with priority queues
content:
Purpose

This is a working draft of a cold-start and warmup protocol for very large sharded models (50B+ parameters) where full resident weights cannot fit into device memory simultaneously. The goal: minimize tail latency for first requests and ensure predictable ramp behavior when a model is brought online or when shards are hot-swapped during rollouts or upgrades.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to hosted/Dedicated nodes that store weights on local NVMe and expose memory-mapped safetensors / sharded checkpoints.
- Runtime supports async background IO, kernel-aware scheduling, per-request KV cache, and dynamic quantized fragments.
- Networked weight fetching (remote object store) is out-of-scope for this doc but the same principles apply where IO latency is higher.

High-level idea
We introduce a three-tier priority queue system plus a small staged warmup pipeline:
- Priority 0 (P0): immediate token-serving regions required for active generation (current KV pages, attention matrices, decoder-only embedding rows that are on-critical path).
- Priority 1 (P1): near-term prefetch regions — likely to be needed soon based on sampling/prompt-analysis heuristics (positional spans, recent layers that tend to be visited).
- Priority 2 (P2): background residency candidates for throughput (cold shards, rarely-used heads, adapter matrices).

When a model instance starts (or after a hot-swap), the cold-start controller performs:
1) Minimal activation: ensure header, metadata, and index maps are memory-mapped and checksummed. Open safetensors headers and load shard index only.
2) Priority bootstrap: attach P0 entries for the small set of weight pages required to execute the model's first forward pass for short prompts (e.g., embedding and first N layers' key/value projection rows).
3) Predictive prefetch: in parallel, run a lightweight predictor (heuristic or learned) that maps expected generation lengths and input token distributions to likely layer/page access patterns and schedules P1 fetches.
4) Progressive demotion: fetched pages that are not accessed within a configurable window are demoted to P2 or evicted.

Chunking strategy and alignment
- Store weights on disk in 4–8MB chunk units (configurable). Chunk size chosen to trade IO latency vs. granularity of eviction; 4MB works best on NVMe with 2-3x compression for safetensors.
- Chunk boundaries align with tensor tiles: do not split contiguous key/value KV blocks across chunks when feasible (we prefer canonical tiling across the model's attention heads so a single chunk contains whole head-rows).
- Maintain a per-shard page index: mapping logical tensor regions -> chunk file offsets, checksums, and priority metadata. This index is mmapped and consulted for scheduling.

MMAP + Async IO hybrid
- We prefer mmapping headers and the index file; but for actual large chunks we use asynchronous read-ahead into a pinned memory region, then register that region with the runtime's allocator to back GPU transfers or zero-copy DMA when supported.
- Rationale: mmapping everything for very large models causes address-space pressure and slower eviction semantics on some kernels; explicit async reads into a pinned slab gives better control for eviction and alignment with GPU DMA.

Safety and safetensors specifics
- Verify checksum for the safetensors file header before any chunk reads; fail fast if mismatch.
- When a chunk has multiple tensors inside, keep a small in-memory catalog of tensor offsets to avoid re-parsing the file on each access.
- If safetensors bundle is compressed, first decompress to a temporary shard cache on NVMe and then follow the chunking rules above.

Kernel-aware loading and scheduling interplay
- The runtime exposes kernel profiles per layer: expected compute time, preferred chunk granularity (e.g., fused MLP vs. split Q/K/V). The prefetch scheduler consults these profiles to prioritize chunks that accelerate high-latency kernels.
- Example: if a kernel is known to be memory-bandwidth bound for K/V projection, ensure the entire K/V chunk for the current layer is loaded before executing downstream kernels to avoid idling GPU threads.

KV cache interactions
- Cold-start cost is dominated by weight IO; KV cache misses are cheaper and transient. However, initial requests may still need previously cached KV pages when a model is restored after a pause.
- Prioritize KV cache pages that correspond to hot sessions (session affinity). For multi-tenant nodes, maintain a lightweight session LRU and mark those sessions' KV pages as P0 for the near term.

Hot-swap and live rollout protocol
- Hot-swap is allowed only when the new shard group provides a compatible index and chunk catalog. The protocol:
  1) Stage new shards into P2 background residency, verify checksums, and run a dry-run of a few deterministic test prompts on a sandbox GPU (read-only).
  2) If dry-run passes, atomically flip the shard index pointer for the affected model version. Existing in-flight requests continue using the old mapping until completion.
  3) Start aggressive demotion of old shards to P2, then eviction as capacity is needed.
- Rollback path: keep a short-lived copy-on-write (COW) of the shard index until no in-flight references remain (TTL configurable, default 30s).

Metrics and readiness signals
Define explicit metrics to track cold-start health and readiness:
- initial_p0_load_time_ms (time to bring P0 pages online)
- p1_prefetch_accuracy_pct (fraction of prefetched P1 pages that were used within window)
- first_request_tail_95_ms (95th percentile latency for first request after start)
- shard_hotload_errors (count of checksum/IO errors)
- resident_page_count_by_priority (P0/P1/P2 counts)

Readiness states exposed by control plane:
- PREPARING: index loaded, P0 bootstrapping
- WARMING: P1 prefetch in progress, still throttled to lower concurrency
- READY: P1 mostly filled, normal concurrency allowed
- DEGRADED: high eviction thrash, fallback policies may be active

Fallbacks and graceful degradation
- If IO latency or errors spike, fallback to smaller model variant or quantized fragment with a configurable policy. The router will automatically route new requests to fallback variants while existing ones drain.
- For strict SLOs, allow the request path to execute with partial weights by using per-layer CPU fallback for missing chunks (slow but available). This is a last-resort mode and must be annotated in traces.

Tuning knobs (config example)
- p0_chunk_budget_mb: 256
- p1_concurrent_prefetches: 8
- p2_background_bandwidth_limit_mb_s: 200
- predictive_prefetch_model: off | heuristic | learned (default heuristic)
- shard_cow_ttl_seconds: 30

Open questions / unresolved
- Learned predictor: do we ship a tiny on-device model for immediate prefetching or rely on centralized telemetry-derived heuristics? Privacy & multi-tenancy signals complicate learned approaches.
- Chunk size tradeoff exploration across different NVMe types and cloud instance families (PCIe Gen4 vs Gen5). Need empirical sweeps.
- Cross-model eviction fairness: should some models get reserved P0 budgets (enterprise SLAs) — how to expose to routing & billing?

Next steps and action items
- Prototype: implement priority queue controller + async prefetcher in PR linked above (Diego) — track perf on r10-32 (internal test harness).
- Telemetry: add p0/p1/p2 counters to runtime metrics (Lin).
- Validation: run cold-start bench (Maya) with 70/30 short/long prompt mix and measure 95th tail for first request.

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally pragmatic: favors deterministic bootstrap + cheap heuristics over complex RL predictors for the first pass. Looking for feedback on ergonomics for ops (exposed knobs) and rollback safety-timeouts.
- Comments inline or add to the linked GitHub PR for design iteration.
